transcript.content: Hello, I'm Dr. Smith. It's nice to meet you; what brings you in to see me today?

Nice to meet you too, Dr. Smith. Well, what finally got me to come in is that my concentration has just gotten really unreliable lately. 

I'll be at the clinic reviewing a patient's chart, or even at home just laying out a watercolor wash, and I'll suddenly realize I’ve read the exact same line three times. My mind just wanders off to... well, to everything that could possibly go wrong. It's getting in the way of things, so I figured I needed to talk to someone about it.
Have these difficulties with concentration and your tendency to worry about everything started following a specific life event or change?

Well, yes, actually. It all really started when I began the formal retirement process at the practice. That was... I'd say about a year and three months ago. It's just been going on ever since I started making those arrangements.

When you find yourself worrying about things that could go wrong, are these concerns mostly limited to the changes surrounding your retirement, or do you find yourself feeling equally anxious about many other different areas of your life as well?

It's really spread out to all sorts of things. I mean, the retirement was the trigger, but my mind just keeps circling around everything now. I worry constantly about whether my old patients are actually being looked after properly by the new partners. Then I'll start stressing over the practice handoff and whether it's financially sound, or if I missed some detail in the paperwork. And then... well, I worry a lot about whether I'll just become completely useless once I'm fully retired. It's constant, and honestly, the amount of worry feels out of proportion even to me, but I just can't seem to stop it.
Do you find that you also experience physical sensations like muscle tension, restlessness, or feeling easily fatigued during these times of worry?

Yes, definitely the fatigue. By midafternoon, I just feel completely worn out. And it's... well, it's in a way that taking a nap or having a quiet morning just doesn't fix. It makes even the simple things, like going out to weed the garden or just standing at the easel, feel a lot heavier than they used to.
Do you find that your worry makes it difficult for you to fall asleep or stay asleep at night?

Yes, sleep has become a real issue. Most nights, I get into bed feeling completely exhausted, but... as soon as the house gets quiet, my mind just switches on. I start replaying the patient transfers in my head, or I'll go over the financial details of the practice handoff again and again. It takes me forever to drift off. And even when I finally do get to sleep, I usually end up waking up around four or five in the morning, and I just feel like I never really settled or got any actual rest.
Aside from the fatigue you mentioned, do you often find yourself feeling physically tense, or perhaps restless and unable to sit still?

Not really, no. I mean, I don't find myself pacing around or feeling like I can't just sit in my chair. And I haven't really noticed my muscles feeling tight or tense, either. It's... well, it's mostly just that heavy exhaustion I mentioned earlier.
Do you find that you have been feeling more irritable or short-tempered with people around you lately?

No, I wouldn't say that. I don't think I've been snapping at anyone or feeling unusually short-tempered. The people at the practice and my family... they haven't mentioned anything, and I don't feel any more irritable than usual.
Looking back over the past year or so, would you say that you have experienced these feelings of excessive worry on more days than not?

Yes, definitely more days than not. Really, this has been going on since I started the formal retirement process... which was about a year and three months ago. So it's been pretty consistent since then.
